title: A nilpotent Borel subgroup is the whole connected affine group
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Let $G$ be a smooth connected affine $k$-group scheme of finite type [def-sc-group-scheme, def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and let $B\subseteq G$ be a Borel subgroup [def-sfb-borel-subgroup-scheme], thus a maximal smooth connected solvable closed subgroup scheme [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Assume that $B$ is nilpotent in the following group-scheme sense: there are an integer $m\geq0$ and closed subgroup schemes $B=B_0\supseteq B_1\supseteq\cdots\supseteq B_m=1$ such that for every commutative $k$-algebra $A$, every $0\leq i<m$, $b\in B(A)$ and $x\in B_i(A)$, the commutator $bxb^{-1}x^{-1}$ belongs to $B_{i+1}(A)$. Here $1=\operatorname{Spec}k$ is the trivial subgroup. Then $B=G$ as closed subgroup schemes. No restriction on $\operatorname{char}k$ or $\dim G$ is imposed.

source.place: Proposition 17.23, printed p.359, implication (b) to (c): its proof establishes G=B for a nilpotent Borel B; Section 17b, printed p.353, supplies the connected group-variety and algebraically closed base hypotheses. Nilpotence is the descending central-series convention of Proposition 6.38, printed p.133.

proof.text: Induct on the given central-series length $m$, for all pairs $(G,B)$ in the statement simultaneously. For $m=0$, $B=1$. The identity $G\to G$ is the quotient by the trivial subgroup: its fibres are singleton cosets, it is faithfully flat of finite presentation, and every point lifts. Thus [lem-sfb-borel-quotient-proper-geometry], with $H=1$, makes $G$ proper and integral. Since $G$ is affine, [lem-sc-proper-affine-finite-general] makes $G=\operatorname{Spec}C$ finite over $k$. The integral finite-dimensional $k$-algebra $C$ is a field: multiplication by any nonzero element is an injective endomorphism of a finite-dimensional vector space, hence surjective. Each element of $C$ is algebraic over the algebraically closed field $k$, so $C=k$. Consequently $G=B=1$.

source.place: Proposition 17.23(b) implies (c), printed p.359, base case; A.75(g). Stacks Tag 01WN (morphisms.tex, lemma-finite-proper) supplies proper plus affine implies finite.

proof.text: Assume $m>0$ and set $N=B_{m-1}$. For every $k$-algebra $R$, $n\in N(R)$ and every $R$-algebra $R\prime$, the series hypothesis gives $[b,n_{R\prime}]=1$ for all $b\in B(R\prime)$. Therefore the $R$-group automorphism $\operatorname{Int}(n)$ of $G_R$ restricts to the identity of $B_R$. Apply [lem-sfb-borel-homomorphism-rigidity] with source and target $G$, homomorphisms $\operatorname{Int}(n)$ and $\mathrm{id}$, to obtain $\operatorname{Int}(n)=\mathrm{id}_{G_R}$. Hence $N$ commutes with $G$ on all test algebras, so $N$ is a closed central, in particular normal, subgroup of $G$.

source.place: Propositions 17.21--17.22, printed pp.358--359; applying their centre-inclusion argument to the last central-series term.

proof.text: Use [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry] to form $q:G\to Q=G/N$. It is faithfully flat and finitely presented, has scheme-theoretic kernel $N$, and $Q$ is affine of finite type and smooth and connected. Indeed $G$ is geometrically connected in the sense of that node because $k$ itself is an algebraic closure, and that property passes to $Q$. By [lem-sfb-quotient-borel-torus-images], $D=q(B)$ is a smooth connected Borel subgroup of $Q$. The subgroup correspondence identifies $B$ with $q^{-1}(D)$ because $N\subseteq B$. No smoothness or connectedness of $N$ is required.

source.place: Proposition 17.20, printed pp.357--358, and Theorem 5.28, printed p.105; quotient by a central subgroup as in Proposition 17.23.

proof.text: For $0\leq i\leq m-1$, the subgroup correspondence of [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry] gives a closed subgroup $D_i\subseteq Q$ with $q^{-1}(D_i)=B_i$, since each $B_i$ contains $N$. Thus $D_0=D$ and $D_{m-1}=1$. The restrictions $B_i\to D_i$ are base changes of $q$, so their sections lift fppf locally. For any $k$-algebra $A$, $d\in D(A)$, $x\in D_i(A)$ and $i<m-1$, lift both over a common fppf cover to $b\in B$ and $y\in B_i$. Then $[d,x]=q([b,y])$ belongs to $D_{i+1}$ there, because $[b,y]\in B_{i+1}$. Membership in a closed subscheme descends along this cover: its defining ideal pulls back to zero after a faithfully flat extension only if it was zero already. Hence $[d,x]\in D_{i+1}(A)$. The $D_i$ form a central series of length $m-1$ for $D$, including $D=1$ when $m=1$.

source.place: Proposition 17.23(b) implies (c), printed p.359, quotient of the nilpotent Borel; explicit central-series image argument, using the quotient torsor and subgroup correspondence of Chapter 5.

proof.text: The induction hypothesis now applies to $(Q,D)$ and the series of length $m-1$, giving $D=Q$. By the inverse-image correspondence in [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry], $B=q^{-1}(D)=q^{-1}(Q)=G$ as closed subgroup schemes. This is an equality on all test algebras, including nonreduced ones, and completes the induction.

source.place: Proposition 17.23(b) implies (c), printed p.359, final inverse-image argument.

proof_origin.place: Proposition 17.23(b) implies (c), printed p.359, with Propositions 17.21--17.22 and 17.20. The central-quotient induction is indexed by the supplied series length instead of dimension; this writes quotient nilpotence explicitly and allows nonsmooth intermediate terms.

(3) The quotient node gives Q=G/N smooth and connected (geometrically connected since kbar=k). quotient-borel-torus-images makes D=q(B) Borel, and the correspondence clause gives B=q^-1(D). (4) D_i comes from the correspondence; D_{m-1}=1 since ker q=N; commutators are lifted over fppf covers and membership descends along an injective faithfully flat A->A'. This is genuinely elementary. (5) The induction on m is set up properly and finishes with B=q^-1(Q)=G. Edge cases tested: m=1, repeated trivial terms, G_a, G_m, unitriangular groups, nonreduced mu_p terms.
